NVIDIA L40S is the NVIDIA H100 AI Alternative with a Big Benefit
By Patrick Kennedy -October 31, 20231
NVIDIA H100 or L40S in Supermicro SYS-521GE-TNRT Servers
Something very different with today’s systems is that they are now a full 5U. This is generally because the TDP of each GPU, H100 or L40S is 350W. Commonly, these systems have eight GPUs for around 2.8kW in the GPUs. The other reason is that between the two options, these systems are typically using power in the 4.3-5kW range. That makes them enough for a single server per 208V 30A rack or several servers in a higher-power rack. Density is less challenging with modern AI servers since often power and cooling in racks is the bigger limiter.

Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 7
Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 7
That extra 1U of space allows for more cooling to the GPUs. NVIDIA GPUs and the H100 and L40S follow this lead and typically can use their maximum rated power, but they also usually use less than their rated power on average.

Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 39
Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 39
Supermicro has both Intel Xeon and AMD EPYC versions of the chassis. We had two Intel Xeon versions set up, one with 8x NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 117
Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 117
And the other with the NVIDIA L40S cards.

Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 118
Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 118
You can see that these are set up with only eight cards, but these systems can scale up to 10, as we used in DeepLearning11 way back in the day.

Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 96
Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 96
With PCIe GPU servers, how GPUs are connected is important for things like P2P across a PCIe switch without NVLink, and how well NVIDIA NCCL works on the workload. NCCL is important to scale out jobs to multiple GPUs. The Supermicro SYS-521GE-TNRT uses PCIe Gen5 switches in a dual root configuration. One can see the two PCIe switches under heatsinks on the GPU board, and that board is cabled between the switches and the CPUs in the systems.

Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 63
Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 63
The NVIDIA H100’s can be installed in this server using the NVLink bridge connecting cards in pairs. Looking at the L40S, everything is PCIe.

Performance Summary
We ran LLaMA 7B inference on these GPUs. We only had a very short amount of time where we had access to them, so that limited what we ran. NVIDIA publishes a lot of numbers for AI, so feel free to browse those. We will hopefully get to update this piece with a few more over time.

NVIDIA L40S Vs H100 LLaMA 7B Inference Performance
NVIDIA L40S Vs H100 LLaMA 7B Inference Performance
We checked our results versus NVIDIA’s official numbers. On the official results, NVIDIA is using its H100 SXM5, not the PCIe version, but we use a rule of thumb that the SXM5 version is around 25% faster (but it varies based on workload) than the PCIe version and it feels like we are in the ballpark.

That brings us to the obvious: why the L40S if the H100 is faster? It turns out that folks are deploying these because 48GB is enough memory, especially using FP8, to be more than competitive with the A100, even the SXM version, using FP16. On the other hand, we generally see a H100 PCIe is 2.0-2.7x the speed of the L40S, but it is also 2.6x the price. The L40S is also available much sooner than the H100, and some deal pricing put the L40S at a level even more competitive with the H100, tipping the scales even more in favor of the L40S.

Patrick With NVIDIA H100 And L40S 1
Patrick With NVIDIA H100 And L40S 1
There are a few caveats. If you are deploying over 10,000 GPUs, NVIDIA is focusing on not just the H100 but also the H100 SXM5 in the Delta Next platforms with NVSwitch and other technologies. We asked NVIDIA about this, and if you are “only” deploying 4000 GPUs (likely ~$50M+ of hardware), for example, the L40S is the go-to solution.

Other Considerations of the NVIDIA L40S vs. H100
There are several other aspects to consider on the L40S. One is that it supports NVIDIA Virtual GPU vGPU 16.1, whereas the H100 is still only supported with vGPU 15. NVIDIA is splitting its AI chips a bit from the vGPU support side.

NVIDIA Virtual GPU Software Supported GPUs As Of 2023 10 31
NVIDIA Virtual GPU Software Supported GPUs As Of 2023 10 31
For those who want to deploy one kind of GPU machine and then be able to run different types of workloads, then something like the L40S makes sense. It also has the NVIDIA video encoding engines with AV1 support and RT cores, given its visualization roots.

Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 7
Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 7
There is one feature the L40S does not support, and that is MIG. We have looked at MIG previously, but it allows a H100 to be split into up to 7 partitions of different sizes. This is mostly useful to split the H100 GPU in public clouds so that the GPU resources can be shared across customers. For an enterprise, this is usually a lower-excitement feature.

NVIDIA A100 40GB Split To Two MIG Instances
NVIDIA A100 40GB Split To Two MIG Instances
Also, deploying the L40S is a lower power affair, half the power of the SXM5 systems. That makes it very attractive for those who want to scale out but may not have huge power budgets for each rack.

Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT 49
Supermicro SYS 521GE TNRT with NVIDIA L40S
The bottom line is that the L40S is not as fast as the H100, but it with its FP8 and Transformer Engine support from NVIDIA, it is an option that is more available and easier to deploy for many than the H100, and often at a lower cost.

Final Words
There is a lot of really poor information out there on the NVIDIA H100 PCIe versus the L40S and why one would use either version. Hopefully, this helps clear that up to a larger extent. To us, the L40S does not feel inexpensive, but it reminds us of 6+ years ago when the thing to do in AI was to use lower-cost NVIDIA GPUs in servers but then use more of them. NVIDIA has that model again, using the L40S and an officially sanctioned architecture that supports up to several thousand GPUs.

NVIDIA H100 L40S A100 Stack Top 1
NVIDIA H100 L40S A100 Stack Top 1
A quick thank you to Supermicro and NVIDIA for supporting this one. This seems to be a question we have been getting, along with simply what is a good H100 alternative architecture that is still NVIDIA. The L40S is really the answer for many customers.

Student: Please integrate (y dx + x dy + 1 dz) along a straight path from (0, 0, 0) to (1, 1, 1)

Tutor: To integrate the given differential form \(y dx + x dy + 1 dz\) along a straight path from \((0, 0, 0)\) to \((1, 1, 1)\), we can parameterize the path and then perform the integration.

A straight path \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) from \((0,0,0)\) to \((1,1,1)\) can be represented as a line segment parameterized by \(t\), with \(0 \leq t \leq 1\), where
\[
\mathbf{r}(t) = t\mathbf{i} + t\mathbf{j} + t\mathbf{k}.
\]

This corresponds to the functions \(x(t) = t\), \(y(t) = t\), and \(z(t) = t\). We also compute the differentials:
\[
dx = dt,\quad dy = dt,\quad dz = dt.
\]

Thus, the line integral becomes the following single-variable integral:
\[
\int_{\text{path}} (y dx + x dy + 1 dz) = \int_0^1 (t dt + t dt + 1 dt) = \int_0^1 (2t + 1) dt.
\]

Now we find the antiderivative of \(2t + 1\):
\[
\int (2t + 1) dt = t^2 + t + C,
\]
where \(C\) is the constant of integration. Since we are performing a definite integral, we don't need to consider \(C\) here.

Evaluating the definite integral from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 1\):
\[
\int_0^1 (2t + 1) dt = [t^2 + t]_0^1 = (1^2 + 1) - (0^2 + 0) = 1 + 1 = 2.
\]

Student: Please derive the formula for curvature that includes the term x''y' - y''x'

Tutor: The formula for curvature \( \kappa \) of a planar curve described by parametric equations \( x(t) \) and \( y(t) \), where \( t \) is the parameter, is indeed expressed as:

\[
\kappa = \frac{|x''(t)y'(t) - y''(t)x'(t)|}{(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}
\]

Here is a derivation of this formula.

For a plane curve described by parametric equations \( x(t) \), \( y(t) \), where \( t \) is the parameter, the curvature at a point is a measure of how quickly the curve is changing direction at that point. It is defined as:

\[
\kappa = \frac{d\theta}{ds}
\]

where \( \theta \) is the angle of the tangent line to the curve with respect to the x-axis, and \( ds \) is the differential arc length. To compute \( d\theta \), note that the tangent vector \( T \) has components \( T = (x'(t), y'(t)) \). If we differentiate \( T \) with respect to \( t \), we get the rate at which the tangent changes, which is proportional to the normal vector \( N \).

Now, the magnitude of the rate of change of the tangent is equal to the magnitude of the derivative of the unit tangent vector, which is given by the curvature \( \kappa \). If we denote the unit tangent vector by \( T \) and its derivative with respect to \( t \) as \( T' \), the relationship between these quantities is:

\[
\kappa = |T'|
\]

Now, express \( T \) as:

\[
T = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}}(x'(t), y'(t))
\]

Differentiating \( T \) with respect to \( t \) gives:

\[
T' = \frac{d}{dt} \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}}(x'(t), y'(t))\right)
\]

Using the product rule and chain rule to differentiate, this becomes:

\[
T' = \frac{1}{(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}} 
\left( (x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)(x''(t), y''(t)) - (x'(t)x''(t) + y'(t)y''(t))(x'(t), y'(t)) \right)
\]

We are interested in the magnitude of \( T' \):

\[
|T'| = \kappa = \frac{1}{(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}} 
\left| (x'(t)y''(t) - y'(t)x''(t)) \right|
\]

And that is the curvature of a plane curve defined by the parametric equations \( x(t) \) and \( y(t) \):

\[
\kappa = \frac{|x''(t)y'(t) - y''(t)x'(t)|}{(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}
\]

This formula tells you how sharply the curve bends at a given point \( t \): the greater the curvature, the sharper the turn. It includes both the second derivatives of \( x \) and \( y \), and their first derivatives as well, which factor into how the tangent vector to the curve is rotating.

Tutor: I apologize for any confusion caused. Let's re-examine the calculation of the derivative of the unit tangent vector \( T \) and its magnitude.

Given the tangent vector \( T = (x'(t), y'(t)) \), the unit tangent vector (when both \( x'(t) \) and \( y'(t) \) are not zero) is:

\[
\hat{T} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}}(x'(t), y'(t))
\]

Now, to get the derivative of \( \hat{T} \), denoted by \( \hat{T}' \), we need to apply the product rule. Let's denote \( \|\hat{T}\| \equiv \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2} \) to simplify notation.

The derivative of \( \hat{T} \) with respect to \( t \) is:

\[
\hat{T}' = \frac{d}{dt} \left(\frac{1}{\|\hat{T}\|}(x'(t), y'(t))\right)
\]

Applying the product rule and chain rule, the derivative of \( \hat{T} \) is:

\[
\hat{T}' = \frac{-1}{\|\hat{T}\|^3}(x'(t), y'(t))(x'(t)x''(t) + y'(t)y''(t)) + \frac{1}{\|\hat{T}\|}(x''(t), y''(t))
\]

Now we can group terms and simplify:

\[
\hat{T}' = \frac{1}{\|\hat{T}\|^3}((x''(t)\|\hat{T}\|^2 - x'(t)(x'(t)x''(t) + y'(t)y''(t)), y''(t)\|\hat{T}\|^2 - y'(t)(x'(t)x''(t) + y'(t)y''(t)))
\]

Notice that I included a negative sign before the first term, because the derivative of \( \frac{1}{\|\hat{T}\|} \) with respect to \( t \) introduces a negative sign due to the chain rule.

Further simplifying:

\[
\hat{T}' = \frac{1}{\|\hat{T}\|^3}(x''(t)\|\hat{T}\|^2 - x'(t)^2x''(t) - x'(t)y'(t)y''(t), y''(t)\|\hat{T}\|^2 - y'(t)^2y''(t) - x'(t)y'(t)x''(t))
\]

Since \( \|\hat{T}\|^2 = x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2 \), we can replace it:

\[
\hat{T}' = \frac{1}{\|\hat{T}\|^3}(x''(t)(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2) - x'(t)^2x''(t) - x'(t)y'(t)y''(t), y''(t)(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2) - y'(t)^2y''(t) - x'(t)y'(t)x''(t))
\]

Simplify the terms:

\[
\hat{T}' = \frac{1}{\|\hat{T}\|^3}(x''(t)y'(t)^2 - x'(t)y'(t)y''(t), y''(t)x'(t)^2 - x'(t)y'(t)x''(t))
\]

When we compute the magnitude of the vector \( \hat{T}' \), cross-term magnitudes cancel out:

\[
|\hat{T}'| = \frac{|x''(t)y'(t) - y''(t)x'(t)|}{(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}
\]

Notice that the \( x'(t)^2x''(t) \) and \( y'(t)^2y''(t) \) terms cancel, and we are left with the terms \( x''(t)y'(t)^2 \) and \( y''(t)x'(t)^2 \), which after simplifying give us the desired expression. The remaining terms represent the determinant of the first and second derivatives vector, which is key in the final formula of curvature.

So, the curvature of the curve is:

\[
\kappa(t) = |\hat{T}'| = \frac{|x''(t)y'(t) - y''(t)x'(t)|}{(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2)^{3/2}}
\]

Student: How do I compute the volume of a cone with radius a and height h using spherical polars

Tutor:
Output:
To compute the volume of a cone with radius \( a \) and height \( h \) using spherical polars, we can use the formula for the volume of a sphere, which is \( V_{sphere} = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \), and subtract the volumes of two cones that together make up the cone.

First, let's calculate the volume of the full sphere:

\[
V_{sphere} = \frac{4}{3}\pi a^3
\]

Next, we need to find the volume of one of the cones. A cone with radius \( a \) and height \( h \) has a base area of \( \pi a^2 \) and a slant height of \( \sqrt{a^2 + h^2} \). The volume of the cone is given by:

\[
V_{cone} = \frac{1}{3} \pi a^2 h
\]

To find the total volume of the cone, we add the volume of the full sphere and the volume of the two cones:

\[
V_{total} = V_{sphere} + 2V_{cone}
\]

Substituting the expressions for the volumes of the sphere and the cone, we get:

\[
V_{total} = \frac{4}{3}\pi a^3 + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{3} \pi a^2 h
\]

Simplifying further:

\[
V_{total} = \frac{4}{3}\pi a^3 + \frac{2}{3} \pi a^2 h
\]

Therefore, the total volume of the cone is:

\[
V_{total} = \frac{4}{3}\pi a^3 + \frac{2}{3} \pi a^2 h
\]

x = \frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{5^2 - 4 \cdot 2 \cdot (-6)}}{2 \cdot 2}
\]

Simplifying inside the square root:

x = \frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{25 + 48}}{4}
\]

\]

Thus, the solutions to the equation are:

Student: what is the earliest age you can test for ADHD in texas. Also, what is the process to request this ADHD test for a 4 year old in texas. 

Tutor: In Texas, ADHD testing can begin as early as preschool age, around 4 to 5 years old. To request an ADHD test for a 4-year-old, follow these steps:

1. Consult with your child's pediatrician: Share your concerns about your child's behavior or development, and the pediatrician can provide guidance on whether ADHD testing is appropriate.

2. Receive a referral for an evaluation: If the pediatrician believes an evaluation is necessary, they can refer you to a psychologist, psychiatrist, or another qualified professional experienced in diagnosing ADHD in young children.

3. Schedule an evaluation: Contact the referred specialist to schedule a comprehensive evaluation, which may include interviews, questionnaires, observation, and testing to assess your child's cognitive, behavioral, and emotional functioning.

4. Follow up with the specialist: After the evaluation, the specialist will discuss the results and any recommended treatment or support if a diagnosis of ADHD is made.

Keep in mind that diagnosing ADHD in very young children can be challenging, as many children exhibit high energy levels and impulsivity at this age. However, early intervention can be beneficial for those with ADHD, so discussing your concerns with a healthcare professional is an essential first step.

Student: how does the concept of "universal basic income" fit into the broader discussion of social welfare?

Tutor: Universal Basic Income (UBI) is a concept that aims to provide a regular, unconditional sum of money from the government to all citizens regardless of their income level. While UBI has been proposed as a potential solution to poverty and inequality, it also raises significant debates within the broader discussion of social welfare. Some arguments against UBI include:

1. Cost: Implementing UBI would require substantial financial resources, which could strain taxpayers' budgets.

2. Effectiveness: There is limited evidence to suggest that UBI would reduce poverty or increase happiness among recipients.

3. Accessibility: UBI might not be feasible for low-income families due to lack of access to financial assistance programs.

4. Equity: UBI could exacerbate existing inequalities if it disproportionately benefits the wealthy.

On the other hand, proponents argue that UBI could alleviate poverty, provide a safety net for vulnerable populations, and promote fairness and equality. They believe that it could reduce the burden on taxpayers and improve overall well-being.

It's worth noting that the debate surrounding UBI is complex and multifaceted, involving considerations of cost, effectiveness, equity, and the distribution of benefits. Ultimately, the decision to implement UBI should take into account the specific needs and circumstances of the community it is intended to serve.

Student: What are the implications of the COVID-19 pandemic on the future of work?

Tutor: The COVID-19 pandemic has had far-reaching implications on the future of work. As we navigate this global health crisis, it's essential to consider the potential impacts on employment and the workforce. Some key implications include:

1. Remote work: With the rise of remote work, companies may need to adapt to new working arrangements and potentially shift their workforce to remote locations.

2. Job displacement: The pandemic has highlighted the vulnerability of certain industries and jobs to disruptions caused by lockdowns and social distancing measures.

3. Skill requirements: The pandemic has accelerated the adoption of digital technologies and skills, requiring workers to develop new competencies and adaptability.

4. Globalization: The pandemic has exposed the interconnectedness of economies and the need for international collaboration and cooperation.

5. Workplace flexibility: Remote work and flexible schedules have become more common, offering greater work-life balance and reducing burnout.

6. Economic recovery: The pandemic has spurred economic growth, leading to increased demand for labor and job opportunities.

7. Long-term effects: The pandemic has raised questions about the long-term impact on employment and the ability to adapt to changing job markets.

As we move forward, it's crucial to consider the potential long-term implications of the pandemic on the workforce and explore strategies for supporting workers during this time.

Student: what are the implications of the COVID-19 pandemic on the future of education?

1. Distance learning: The pandemic has necessitated the use of online platforms for education, leading to a shift towards distance learning.

2. Increased focus on technology: Schools have prioritized the use of technology to enhance student engagement and facilitate learning.

3. Online assessments: The pandemic has led to the widespread use of online assessments and evaluations to measure student progress.

4. Increased emphasis on STEM subjects: Many schools have shifted their curriculum to emphasize science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) subjects.

5. Collaboration and partnerships: The pandemic has highlighted the importance of collaboration and partnerships between schools, teachers, and students.

6. Increased focus on mental health: Schools have adapted to the new normal, with increased emphasis on mental health support and counseling services.

7. Future-proofing education: The pandemic has underscored the need for future-proofing education, ensuring that it can withstand future challenges and changes.

As we navigate this period of change, it's essential to consider the potential long-term implications of the pandemic on the future of education and explore strategies for supporting educators, students, and institutions during this time.

Термин “Mind” на английском языке представляет значительные сложности при переводе на русский язык. Он охватывает круг явлений, для которого не существует единого обозначения на русском языке. Речь идет обо всем, что происходит “в голове человека”, за исключением материальных процессов, таких как кровообращение, изменение электрических потенциалов и т.д. В русском языке для обозначения этого круга явлений употребляются такие слова, как “психика, сознание, разум, дух”, а также соответствующие прилагательные. В данном контексте термин “Mind” используется преимущественно как эквивалент “мира 2” по Попперу, а также в применении к Попперовскому миру 3.

В предметном указателе к английскому оригиналу этой книги, первое издание которой вышло в 1972 году, термин “Mind” не имеет самостоятельной статьи и отсылает к словам “сознание, состояние (мыслительное), мир 2” и “тело-дух”. Следовательно, его следует переводить в основном как “сознание” с возможным исключением для контекста обсуждения проблемы “тело-дух”.

Однако в некоторых случаях перевод “Mind” как “дух” кажется единственно возможным, особенно в контексте дуализма тела и духа, например, в начале главы 4. В других контекстах перевод “Mind” как “разум” представляется также допустимым или даже предпочтительным, особенно в связи с понятием Попперовского мира 3, который определяется как мир идей и возможных предметов мысли.

In general, the idea of reality and history as something objective and existing is gradually disappearing in consciousness, "reality is agonizing. Now even the opposition between the real and the unreal - the cornerstone of culture - is in question, and the ground is slipping away from under the feet of the fantastic: one cannot undermine the credibility of what is no longer trusted. Transgression is a key concept of postmodernism, capturing the phenomenon of crossing an impassable boundary, above all the boundary between the possible and the impossible. Transformed reality or its frontier (limit) and transgression (qualitative transformation, extension of reality, unreality) are fundamental components in Popper's work, enabling the study of boundary shifts and cultural transformations

known that most philosophical concepts are multi-dimensional. From the
point of view of the requirements of rigor and accuracy of scientific terminology, multivalued is a disadvantage that must be avoided. However, in a
philosophical text multi-variance can be manifested as an insufficient development of the formal and logical structure of the concept, it can become a
support for reflection — for comprehension of a philosophical concept in
different aspects and meanings. The essence of work of the translator of
postmodern philosophical texts consists in selection of translation strategies
by means of which he can fully and correctly transfer the sense of complex
philosophical concepts to another language.
Thus, we can conclude that a postmodern philosophical term is a unique
language unit. It has such qualities as non-objectivity, polysemy and "inseparability" from the non-technological meaning of the term. In addition, it allows for many interpretations and is defined solely by the context of the
whole text and the author's philosophical concept.

Tutor: Below is a list of various seismic scales, divided into objective and subjective categories:

Subjective Scales (Macroseismic Scales): These scales focus on the effects of earthquakes on people, structures, and natural features based on observed damages and human experiences.

1. Rossi-Forel Scale (RF): Developed in 1883, it's an early macroseismic intensity scale with 10 degrees of intensity.
2. Mercalli Scale: The original scale was created in 1902 by Giuseppe Mercalli, which was later modified in 1931.
3. Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) Scale: Based on the Mercalli Scale and modified by Harry O. Wood and Frank Neumann in 1931, it has 12 intensity levels expressed in Roman numerals (I to XII).
4. Medvedev-Sponheuer-Karnik (MSK) Scale: Introduced in 1964 with 12 intensity levels (I to XII). It's an improvement over the Mercalli Scale, considering building types along with other factors.
5. European Macroseismic Scale (EMS-98): A more advanced macroseismic scale, introduced in 1998 with 12 levels (I to XII), taking buildings' vulnerability and standardized damage scales into account.

Objective Scales (Seismological Scales): These scales measure parameters that directly relate to the energy released during an earthquake, such as amplitude and frequency.

1. Richter Scale: Developed in 1935 by Charles Richter, the scale measures the magnitude of an earthquake using the base-10 logarithm of the ground shaking's amplitude (A) in micrometers, recorded by a seismograph. Formula: M_Richter = log10(A) – log10(A₀), where A₀ is the reference amplitude.

2. Moment Magnitude Scale (Mw): Introduced in 1979 as an updated version of the Richter Scale, Mw derives the magnitude from the seismic moment. Formula: M_W = (2/3) * log10(M₀) - 10.7, where M₀ is the seismic moment in Newton-meters (Nm).

3. Body Wave Magnitude (mb): A short-period magnitude scale that measures body wave (P wave) amplitude. Formula: m_b = log10(A/T) + Q(Δ) + 1.17*ε, where A and T are the amplitude and period of the maximum P wave, Q(Δ) is the correction for the epicentral distance (Δ), and ε accounts for the focal depth.

4. Surface Wave Magnitude (Ms): A long-period magnitude scale that measures surface wave (Rayleigh and Love wave) amplitude. Formula: M_s = log10(A/T) + 1.656*log10(Δ) + 2.2, where A and T are the amplitude and period of the maximum surface wave, and Δ is the epicentral distance.

5. Energy Magnitude (Me): A scale based on the total radiated seismic energy (E) of an earthquake. Formula: M_e = (2/3)*(log10(E) -4.4), where E is the seismic energy in Joules (J).

Please note that calculating seismic magnitudes often involves additional correction factors and variations in formulas based on the seismograph type and other parameters, so these formulas may be simplified versions of the actual methods used.

class PIDController:

    def __init__(self, kp, ki, kd, limit):
        self.kp = kp
        self.ki = ki
        self.kd = kd
        self.limit = limit
        self.prev_error = 0
        self.integral = 0

    def update(self, error, dt):
        derivative = (error - self.prev_error) / dt
        self.integral += error * dt
        self.integral = max(min(self.integral, self.limit), -self.limit)  # Clamp the integral term
        output = self.kp * error + self.ki * self.integral + self.kd * derivative
        self.prev_error = error
        return output

    vy = (dy / distance) * speed
    vz = (dz / distance) * speed
    return vx, vy, vz

Tutor: 1. Two Egyptian brands that have gone international are "Cottonil" and "Juhayna". 

Cottonil is a well-known Egyptian brand that deals with cotton underwear and garments. The brand was established in 1994 and is now internationally recognized for its quality products. Cottonil has expanded its presence in several countries, including Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman, and Jordan.

Juhayna is one of the leading dairy and juice companies in Egypt. The brand was founded in 1983 and has since grown to become a significant player in the Middle Eastern market. Juhayna exports its products to several countries, such as Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Yemen, Sudan, Libya, Jordan, and Palestine.

2. Entry Strategy, Entry Orientation, and Introduction Strategy for the 4Ps of Cottonil and Juhayna:

Cottonil:
- Entry Strategy: Franchising and wholly-owned subsidiaries
- Entry Orientation: Market development
- Introduction Strategy: Cottonil emphasizes product quality and affordability in their 4Ps: product, price, place, and promotion.

Juhayna:
- Entry Strategy: Direct Export and strategic alliances
- Entry Orientation: Market penetration
- Introduction Strategy: Juhayna focuses on product differentiation and innovation in their 4Ps: product, price, place, and promotion.

3. International Strategy for each element and changes in the domestic environment:

Cottonil:
- Product: Cottonil maintains the same three levels of their product (core, actual, and augmented) in both local and international markets. Their strategy is to offer high-quality products to the customers. They did not change the three levels in the domestic environment.
- Product Element Strategy: Standardization strategy, as they provide the same high-quality products in all markets without much change.

Juhayna:
- Product: Juhayna also maintains the same three levels of their product (core, actual, and augmented) in both local and international markets. Their strategy is to offer innovative and differentiated products to the customers. They did not change the three levels in the domestic environment.
- Product Element Strategy: Adaptation strategy, as they adjust their products according to the local market needs and preferences.

4. Pricing element and strategy:

Cottonil:
- Pricing Strategy: Penetration pricing, where they offer their products at lower prices to gain market share in the international markets.
- Determinants of Pricing: Production cost, marketing expenses, and exchange rate fluctuations.

Juhayna:
- Pricing Strategy: Competitive pricing, where they set their prices in line with the competitors' prices to attract more customers.
- Determinants of Pricing: Production cost, marketing expenses, competitors' prices, and exchange rate fluctuations.

Cottonil:
- Place Element: Franchised stores and wholly-owned subsidiaries in various countries in the Middle East.
- Market Coverage Goal: Cottonil aims to expand its presence in the international market and become a leading brand in the underwear and garment industry.

Juhayna:
- Place Element: Direct Export through strategic alliances with local distributors and retailers.
- Market Coverage Goal: Juhayna aims to penetrate the new markets and increase its market share in the existing markets to become a leading player in the dairy and juice industry.

in the system is the sum of the time spent by this job in waiting plus the time
spent on its execution.)
Design a greedy algorithm for this problem. Does the greedy algorithm
always yield an optimal solution?

the same resource, the task is to find the largest number of these intervals so
that no two of them overlap. Investigate the three greedy algorithms based on
a. earliest start first.
b. shortest duration first.
c. earliest finish first.
For each of the three algorithms, either prove that the algorithm always yields
an optimal solution or give a counterexample showing this not to be the case.

operation: take two of the vessels and split the total amount of water in them
equally between them. The object is to achieve a minimum amount of water
in the vessel containing all the water in the initial set up by a sequence of such
operations. What is the best way to do this?

4)Rumor spreading There are n people, each in possession of a different
rumor. They want to share all the rumors with each other by sending electronic
messages. Assume that a sender includes all the rumors he or she knows at
the time the message is sent and that a message may only have one addressee.
Design a greedy algorithm that always yields the minimum number of
messages they need to send to guarantee that every one of them gets all the
rumors.

Greedy Algorithm: Schedule jobs in increasing order of their duration.
1. Sort jobs by their durations t1, t2, ..., tn.
2. Execute jobs in sorted order.

The greedy algorithm always yields an optimal solution. To prove this, consider two adjacent jobs Ji and Jj with durations ti and tj respectively in the sorted order such that ti <= tj. If we swap these two jobs, the waiting time for Ji will increase by tj - ti, while the waiting time for Jj will decrease by ti. Hence, the total waiting time will not decrease. Therefore, the algorithm is optimal.

2) Compatible Intervals

a. Earliest start first
Algorithm: Schedule intervals with the earliest start time first.
1. Sort intervals by their start times a1, a2, ..., an.
2. Select the interval with the earliest start time.
3. Remove all overlapping intervals and repeat step 2 until no intervals are left.

Counterexample: Consider intervals (1,5), (2,3), and (4,6). The optimal solution is to select intervals (2,3) and (4,6), but the earliest start first algorithm will select (1,5) and exclude the other two intervals.

b. Shortest duration first
Algorithm: Schedule intervals with the shortest duration first.
1. Sort intervals by their durations (b1-a1), (b2-a2), ..., (bn-an).
2. Select the interval with the shortest duration.
3. Remove all overlapping intervals and repeat step 2 until no intervals are left.

Counterexample: Consider intervals (1,4), (2,3), (4,5), and (6,7). The optimal solution is to select intervals (1,4), (4,5), and (6,7), but the shortest duration first algorithm will select (2,3) and exclude (1,4) and (4,5).

c. Earliest finish first
Algorithm: Schedule intervals with the earliest finish time first.
1. Sort intervals by their finish times b1, b2, ..., bn.
2. Select the interval with the earliest finish time.
3. Remove all overlapping intervals and repeat step 2 until no intervals are left.

The earliest finish first algorithm always yields an optimal solution. To prove this, consider an interval Ii in the optimal solution. There must be an interval Ij that finishes no later than Ii. If Ij is not in the optimal solution, then we can replace Ii with Ij and still have a valid solution. Therefore, the earliest finish first algorithm is optimal.

3) Averaging Down

The best way to achieve a minimum amount of water in the vessel containing all the water is to divide the water into smaller equal portions by performing the operation as many times as possible.

Algorithm:
1. Start with the vessel containing W pints of water and the rest empty.
2. Select two vessels, one containing water and another empty.
3. Split the water equally between the two vessels.
4. Repeat the process until all n vessels have water.

After performing the operation n-1 times, each vessel will have W/n pints of water, which is the minimum amount possible.

Greedy Algorithm: Each time, select a person who knows the most rumors and send messages to others who don't know them yet.

Algorithm:
1. Start with each person knowing only their rumor.
2. Find the person with the most rumors known.
3. Send messages to others who don't know these rumors.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until everyone knows all the rumors.

The algorithm always yields a minimum number of messages needed to guarantee that everyone gets all the rumors. The process of selecting the person with the most rumors ensures that we maximize the number of rumors disseminated in a single message, and this will minimize the total number of messages sent.

Student: Explain Leipzig interlinear glossing:
What four lines typically appear together?
How are content morphemes and grammatical morphemes glossed?
What’s the difference between a space, a minus, and an equals sign placed between the morphemes?
What is the period used for?
Do the morphemes in the source text and gloss have to line up?
What’s the difference between part of speech tagging and glossing?

Tutor: Leipzig Glossing Rules provide a standardized system for the interlinear glossing of linguistic examples. When using these rules, four lines typically appear together:

1. The original language example (source text)
2. The morpheme-by-morpheme breakdown (morphemic segmentation)
3. The gloss for each morpheme, indicating their meaning or grammatical function
4. The free translation of the entire sentence or phrase

Content morphemes (lexical morphemes) and grammatical morphemes (functional morphemes) are glossed using different conventions:

- Content morphemes are glossed with a direct lexical translation. These include nouns, verbs, adjectives, and some adverbs that carry the main semantic load of a sentence.
- Grammatical morphemes are glossed with abbreviations that explain their grammatical function. These include affixes and particles that signify tense, mood, case, number, etc.

In the gloss line, different separators are used to indicate the relationships between morphemes:

- A space indicates a boundary between separate words.
- A hyphen (-) is used to separate bound morphemes, such as affixes, from the roots to which they are attached.
- An equals sign (=) marks clitics, which are grammatical elements that behave as a single phonological unit but have a syntactic or morphological association with other words.

The period (.) is often used to indicate morpheme boundaries within a single word where the morphemes can stand alone or may have their own syntactic properties.

The morphemes in the source text and gloss are ideally aligned horizontally to allow a reader to draw a one-to-one correspondence between the source and its analysis. This helps to clearly illustrate which part of the source text relates to which part of the gloss.

Part of speech tagging and glossing are related but distinct practices:

- Part of speech tagging involves assigning labels to words in a sentence to indicate their grammatical category, such as noun, verb, adjective, etc., without providing a translation or explicit semantic information.
- Glossing, especially as done with Leipzig rules, not only offers equivalent terms for the morphemes from the original language but also includes grammatical information, typically represented in the form of standardized abbreviations and symbols that denote the grammatical functions.

Glossing provides a deeper level of analysis and translation that can reveal the structure and meaning more transparently for students and researchers who may not be familiar with the language being analyzed.

Text:“Tender is the Night” by F. Scott Fitzgerald / Chapter XIII
Dick turned the corner of the traverse and continued along the trench walking on the duckboard. He came to a periscope, looked through it a moment; then he got up on the step and peered over the parapet. In front of him beneath a dingy sky was Beaumont Hamel; to his left the tragic hill of Thiepval. Dick stared at them through his field glasses, his throat straining with sadness.
He went on along the trench, and found the others waiting for him in the next traverse. He was full of excitement and he wanted to communicate it to them, to make them understand about this, though actually Abe North had seen battle service and he had not.
“This land here cost twenty lives a foot that summer,” he said to Rosemary. She looked out obediently at the rather bare green plain with its low trees of six years’ growth. If Dick had added that they were now being shelled she would have believed him that afternoon. Her love had reached a point where now at last she was beginning to be unhappy, to be desperate. 
***
     They came out of the neat restored trench, and faced a memorial to the Newfoundland dead. Reading the inscription Rosemary burst into sudden tears. Like most women she liked to be told how she should feel, and she liked Dick’s telling her which things were ludicrous and which things were sad. But most of all she wanted him to know how she loved him, now that the fact was upsetting everything, now that she was walking over the battle-field in a thrilling dream.
     After that they got into their car and started back to toward Amiens. A thin warm rain was falling on the new scrubby woods and underbrush and they passed great funeral pyres of sorted duds, shells, bombs, grenades, and equipment, helmets, bayonets, gun stocks and rotten leather, abandoned six years in the ground. And suddenly around a bend the white caps of a great sea of graves. Dick asked the chauffer to stop.
     “There’s that girl – and still with her wreath.”
     They watched as he got out and went over to the girl, who stood uncertainly by the gate with a wreath in her hand. Her taxi waited. She was a red-haired girl from Tennessee whom they had met on the train this morning, come from Knoxville to lay a memorial on her brother’s grave. There were tears of vexation on her face.
     “The War Department must have given me the wrong number,” she whimpered. “It had another name on it. I been lookin’ for it since two o’clock, and there’s so many graves.”
     “Then if I were you I’d lay it on any grave without looking at the name,” Dick advised her.
     “You reckon that’s what I ought to do?”
     “I think that’s what he’d have wanted you to do.”
     It was growing dark and the rain was coming down harder. She left the wreath on the first grave inside the gate, and accepted Dick’s suggestion that she dismiss her taxi-cab and ride back to Amiens with them.
     Rosemary shed tears again when she heard of the mishap – altogether it had been a watery day, but she felt that she had learned something, though exactly what it was she did not know. Later she remembered all the hours of the afternoon as happy – one of those uneventful times that seem at the moment only a link between past and future pleasure but turn out to have been the pleasure itself.
     Amiens was an echoing purple town, still sad with the war, as some railroad stations were: - the Gare du Nord and Waterloo station in London. In the daytime one is deflated by such towns, with their little trolley cars of twenty years ago crossing the street gray cobble-stoned squares in front of the cathedral, and the very weather seems to have a quality of the past, faded weather like that of old photographs. But after dark all that is most satisfactory in French life swims back into the picture – the sprightly tarts, the men arguing with a hundred Voilàs in the cafés, the couples drifting, head to head, toward the satisfactory inexpensiveness of nowhere. Waiting for the train they sat in a big arcade, tall enough to release the smoke and chatter and music upward and obligingly the orchestra launched into “Yes, We Have No Bananas,” – they clapped, because the leader looked so pleased with himself. The Tennessee girl forgot her sorrow and enjoyed herself, even began flirtations of tropical eye-rollings and pawings, with Dick and Abe. They teased her gently.
     Then, leaving infinitesimal sections of Wurtemburgers, Prussian Guards, Chausseurd Alpins, Manchester mill hands and old Etonians to pursue their eternal dissolution under the warm rain, they took the train for Paris. They ate sandwiches of mortadel sausage and bel paese cheese made up in the station restaurant, and drank Beaujolais. Nicole was abstracted, biting her lip restlessly and reading over  the guide-books to the battle-field that Dick had brought along – indeed, he had made a quick study of the whole affair, simplifying it always until it bore a faint resemblance to one of his own parties.

Tutor: Title: Grapefruit vs. Banana: A Nutritional Comparison

Introduction

Grapefruit and bananas are both popular fruits among individuals who are keen on maintaining a healthy lifestyle. Nevertheless, these fruits differ significantly in their nutritional benefits. This essay will compare the differences in their nutritional content, focusing on three key areas: protein and amino acid content, vitamins and minerals, and dietary fibers and their effect on gut microbes. Close examination of these three categories will reveal the superiority of one fruit over the other in terms of nutritional aspects.

Body

1) Protein & Amino Acid Content

Protein is an essential macronutrient that plays a crucial role in maintaining normal body functions and tissue repair. Amino acids, on the other hand, are the building blocks of proteins that are necessary for growth and development. Although neither grapefruit nor bananas are rich sources of proteins, their amino acid composition is an important factor to consider. Bananas contain a slightly higher amount of protein, averaging around 1 gram per medium-sized fruit, whereas a half grapefruit has approximately 0.77 grams of protein. Furthermore, bananas contain all nine essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source, while grapefruit is deficient in a few essential amino acids, such as lysine and tryptophan.

2) Vitamins & Minerals

Vitamins and minerals are vital micronutrients that help in various physiological processes in the body. Grapefruits are known for their high vitamin C content, providing nearly 52% of the daily value in just half a medium-sized fruit. This antioxidant vitamin boosts the immune system, protects cells from damage, and promotes collagen synthesis. Besides vitamin C, grapefruits also contain reasonable amounts of vitamin A and potassium, which contribute to maintaining a healthy vision and blood pressure, respectively. Bananas, on the other hand, are famously high in potassium, with a medium-sized fruit providing about 12% of the daily value. They also contain notable amounts of vitamin C, vitamin B6, and manganese, which aid in energy metabolism, hormone regulation, and maintaining strong bones and connective tissues. Overall, grapefruits are superior in terms of their vitamin content, especially in vitamin C, while bananas have a slightly more balanced profile, with significant contributions of potassium, vitamin B6, and manganese.

3) Dietary Fibers & Gut Microbes

Dietary fibers play an essential role in maintaining healthy digestion and promoting a balanced gut microbiota. There are two types of dietary fibers: soluble, which slow digestion and help regulate blood sugar levels, and insoluble, which add bulk to stool and aid in regular bowel movements. While both grapefruits and bananas contain dietary fibers, grapefruits have a higher fiber content, with half a medium-sized fruit providing about 2 grams, compared to 1.1 grams in a banana. Furthermore, grapefruit contains both soluble (pectin) and insoluble (cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin) fibers, with pectin being particularly important for promoting the growth of beneficial gut bacteria. Bananas, on the other hand, primarily contain soluble fiber in the form of resistant starch and pectin, which also support gut health, but may not be as effective as the combination of fibers found in grapefruits.

Conclusion

In conclusion, although both grapefruits and bananas offer numerous health benefits, grapefruits emerge as a superior choice in terms of their protein content, vitamin and mineral profile, and dietary fiber composition. However, it is important to recognize that the nutritional strengths and weaknesses of both fruits should not deter anyone from consuming them in a balanced diet, as each fruit contributes uniquely to overall health and well-being. Future research may also explore the subtleties of these fruits in a more comprehensive manner to understand their full potential as dietary staples.

Grapefruit and Banana are both popular fruits among individuals who are keen on maintaining a healthy lifestyle. Nevertheless, these fruits differ significantly in their nutritional benefits. This essay will compare the differences in their nutritional content, focusing on three key areas: protein and amino acid content, Vitamins and minerals, and dietary fibers & their effect on gut microbes. Close examination of these three categories will reveal the superiority of one fruit over the other in terms of nutritional aspects.

Body

1) Protein & Amino Acid Content

Protein is an essential macronutrient that plays a crucial role in maintaining normal body functions and tissue repair. Amino acids, on the other hand, are the building blocks of proteins that are necessary for growth and development. Although neither grapefruit nor bananas are rich sources of proteins, their amino acid composition is an important factor to consider. Bananas contain a slightly higher amount of protein, averaging around 1 gram per medium-sized fruit, whereas a half grapefruit has approximately 0.77 grams of protein. Furthermore, bananas contain all nine essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source, while grapefruit is deficient in a few essential amino acids, such as lysine and tryptophan.

2) Vitamins & Minerals

Vitamins and minerals are vital micronutrients that help in various physiological processes in the body. Grapefruits are known for their high vitamin C content, providing nearly 52% of the daily value in just half a medium-sized fruit. This antioxidant vitamin boosts the immune system, protects cells from damage, and promotes collagen synthesis. Besides vitamin C, grapefruits also contain reasonable amounts of vitamin A and potassium, which contribute to maintaining a healthy vision and blood pressure, respectively. Bananas, on the other hand, are famously high in potassium, with a medium-sized fruit providing about 12% of the daily value. They also contain notable amounts of vitamin C, vitamin B6, and manganese, which aid in energy metabolism, hormone regulation, and maintaining strong bones and connective tissues. Overall, grapefruits are superior in terms of their vitamin content, especially in vitamin C, while bananas have a slightly more balanced profile, with significant contributions of potassium, vitamin B6, and manganese.

3) Dietary Fibers & Gut Microbes

Dietary fibers play an essential role in maintaining healthy digestion and promoting a balanced gut microbiota. There are two types of dietary fibers: soluble, which slow digestion and help regulate blood sugar levels, and insoluble, which add bulk to stool and aid in regular bowel movements. While both grapefruits and bananas contain dietary fibers, grapefruits have a higher fiber content, with half a medium-sized fruit providing about 2 grams, compared to 1.1 grams in a banana. Furthermore, grapefruit contains both soluble (pectin) and insoluble (cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin) fibers, with pectin being particularly important for promoting the growth of beneficial gut bacteria. Bananas, on the other hand, primarily contain soluble fiber in the form of resistant starch and pectin, which also support gut health, but may not be as effective as the combination of fibers found in grapefruits.

Conclusion

In conclusion, although both grapefruits and bananas offer numerous health benefits, grapefruits emerge as a superior choice in terms of their protein content, vitamin and mineral profile, and dietary fiber composition. However, it is important to recognize that the nutritional strengths and weaknesses of both fruits should not deter anyone from consuming them in a balanced diet, as each fruit contributes uniquely to overall health and well-being. Future research may also explore the subtleties of these fruits in a more comprehensive manner to understand their full potential as dietary staples.

It looked like it would be a defencive battle despite the enemies being in battle formation outside the fort. Sören's uncle, Klaus, stepped forward, quite a distance away from the war camp. There was a great and bright explosion and a titan in its place a few seconds later. The generals and the upper echelon of the military cheered as the titan walked to meet their enemies. The giant had a muscular build, with wide shoulders, thick limbs, and hardened white plates all over its body. Even the eyes, reflecting the sunlight like metal, were armoured. The ground boomed with each step while Klaus walked with confidence.

It would be over soon, the enemies always ended up trampled by the titans. This time, the Founding Titan was not available to help, because another battle, far greater in scale, was being fought on Eldia's southwestern border. The plan was to have the Armoured Titan kill most of the enemies and destroy the fort, followed by the cavalry, which would strike down survivors. Sören simply looked in wonder. He felt a hand touching his shoulder. It was Heinrich, his childhood friend and candidate for the succession of the Beast Titan. His brown beard and hair were overgrown, and his hazel eyes looked energetic despite the general neglect for the body.

— It is simply amazing seeing one of the nine in action, isn't it?

— Indeed. I never tire of seeing how the Armoured takes no damage at all. — Sören replied.

— I just wish we can fight together in the future. You're lucky that your tenure is already guaranteed. — He sighed.

— Is your brother still at it? He doesn't even come to watch the battles.

They suddenly went silent as they looked wide-eyed at the Armoured Titan. He had easily breached the fort walls by simply running into them. The enemy troops were scattered. Arrows and stones were uselessly thrown at him. He destroyed the trebuchets one by one and thoroughly made sure the fort could not be used again by reducing the walls to mere scattered bricks. He signalled with his hand in the distance. The cavalry on the camp moved out, all armed with spears.

— Another victory for Eldia. — Heinrich said.

— As usual. It's good that I won't have to worry about damage when I fight like my uncle in the future.

— Yes, I've heard that previous Jaw Titans were damaged by trebuchet stones. I bet it was simply because of the user's neglect, the Jaw could have easily dodged the projectiles.

As Heinrich talked, Sören's mind thought about other things. His lifespan would be cut short to thirteen more years, he would have to kill without hesitation, his responsibilities would be even greater… If only there was another eligible heir of age. Strangely, the Brandt clan was composed by many children and many elders, and the few adults abstained from inheriting the Armoured.

Heinrich waved his hand over Sören's eyes.

— Are you listening to me?

He stared blankly at Heinrich.

— Have you ever stopped to think that we'll die early? That we'll kill hundreds of thousands?

— Erm… Yes, but why bring it up now? — Heinrich scratched his own head.

— Doesn't that upset you?

— Why? We're doing this for the glory of Eldia! It is as our ancestors wanted. Besides, these other people are inferior to us. Blessed are the subjects of Ymir who can channel part of her power!

Sören decided not to talk anymore. His fate was already decided. Liking it or not, he would inherit the Armoured Titan. The other Eldians in the war camp cheered as Klaus came back, still in titan form. The non-Eldian auxiliaries stood silent, trembling in fear.

— You see that, boy?

Sören turned around to look at the middle-aged man who spoke to him. It was Alexamenos, that despite not being an Eldian, was a high-ranking officer. He apparently was the advisor of a king and tricked the entire court, in the end leading to the Eldian army "peacefully" conquering the kingdom. His greying hair was short, and a stubble covered his lower face.

— You will inherit this power. By Ymir, I wish I was an Eldian like you! — Alexamenos said enthusiastically.

Tutor: The economic system in Nazi Germany from 1934 to 1945 can be best characterized as a form of state-controlled capitalism. The government, under Adolf Hitler's regime, exerted significant influence and control over the economy, while leaving a certain degree of private ownership. This system aimed at achieving self-sufficiency and economic autarky, with the goal of preparing Germany for war.

To achieve economic self-sufficiency, the Nazis pursued a policy known as "Four-Year Plan," which began in 1936. This plan, led by Hermann Göring, aimed to prioritize the development of key industries, such as armaments, steel, and coal, while limiting imports and maximizing domestic production. The government played an active role in directing investment, setting production targets, and establishing cartels to coordinate economic activities.

The Nazi regime also pursued extensive government intervention in labor markets. The German Labor Front (Deutsche Arbeitsfront) replaced trade unions and functioned as a state-controlled labor organization. It aimed to promote the interests of workers while strictly controlling labor relations and preventing strikes. Additionally, the regime implemented policies such as the "Strength Through Joy" program, which encompassed various social welfare measures aimed at winning the support and loyalty of the working class.

The Nazi economic system relied heavily on militarization and war preparation. Massive government spending was directed towards the military-industrial complex, which created both jobs and economic stimulus. The government also established state-owned military-industrial conglomerates, such as the German Labour Front and Hermann Göring Works, to ensure an uninterrupted supply of weapons and promote production efficiency.

Furthermore, the Nazi regime pursued aggressive economic expansionism through territorial conquest. This involved the annexation of Austria, the occupation of Czechoslovakia, and the colonization of other territories during World War II. These actions were fueled by the desire to exploit resources and establish control over occupied regions to bolster the German economy.

It is crucial to acknowledge the immense human suffering, oppression, and atrocities perpetrated by the Nazi regime during this period. While the economic policies pursued under Hitler's totalitarian rule achieved some short-term economic recovery and reduced unemployment, they were ultimately aligned with radical ideologies, militarism, and the pursuit of territorial dominance rather than any sustainable economic principles.

Student: Poetry and prose professions
The editorial staff receives many letters every day. These letters are sincere and frank. One can feel that their authors want to confess and ask for advice. After all, it's easier to tell a stranger everything about yourself, even the most intimate, most cherished things, than it is to your closest friend.
These two letters came at the same time. Both were from girls of the same age. One girl, after graduating from high school, went to work in an office, and she is depressed by the monotony of her simple, but mundane work. She envies those who are always on the road, who sleep in tents, who see the starry sky above them instead of the ceiling.
Another girl became a surveyor. She spends weeks or even months in the field, which is why she misses the bustling city so much, and envies her peers who can go to discos every night, if not to museums and theaters, then at least to discos. She hates her profession. "I think I'm on the wrong train. I should change trains, but it's so hard to do that now," she writes.
Indeed, it is difficult now. Just as it is not easy, after all, to choose the right train on time and correctly. 
What a false and sham idea our young people have about different professions! For them, a doctor is a face in a gauze bandage, a bright lamp over a surgical table. Relatives are waiting at the door of the operating room, already with flowers, because they are convinced that the operation will go well. For young people, a steelmaker is a hard look, a determined expression on a man's face, a bright flame of the open-hearth furnace... A geologist is a backpack, edelweiss, waterfalls, risky but always successful crossings of stormy mountain rivers, a guitar by a picturesque campfire... 
How easy it is to portray the external attributes of professions! And how difficult it is to reveal the true essence of the profession! Here you have to understand the prose of people's daily hard work, because without prose there is no poetry.
The life of a geologist is months, if not years, of processing collected materials. It is off-road, unsettled, often homeless and familyless. In addition to the beauty of mountain gorges and the exoticism of dense thickets, it is fierce mosquitoes and annoying fly flies, and endless fatigue.
The life of a surgeon is a continuous physical and mental strain, healing human wounds and ulcers. It is a daily routine of receiving suffering and sometimes irritated patients, exhausting night shifts.  Often, it is also the most difficult moral duty to tell the family that despite all efforts, it was not possible to save the patient...
A teacher's life is not just armfuls of flowers on exam day. It's piles of notebooks that have to be checked until late at night, noise in the classroom, jostling during breaks, forty students with different, difficult personalities... And there are forty in each class, but how many in total? And in a lifetime?
So look closely at the people, at their work, at the prose and poetry of the professions that interest you! So that you don't have to change trains later.

Student: Suppose I am conducting a research paper on time series data entitled “The Nexus Among Oil Price, Stock Market, and Exchange Rate During Recent Pandemic & Russia-Ukraine Crisis: Fresh Evidence from UK Economy”. Here I have taken three variables Stock Index (SI), Brent Oil Price (OP), and Exchange Rate (ER). I have taken time series data from 2014-2023 segmenting into four periods. 2014-2019 for Pre-covid Period; 2020-2021 for Covid Period; 2022-2023 for War Period and 2014-2023 for the Overall Period. My Research Questions are:
1. Does each variable have a direct influence on others?
2. Does each variable granger cause one another and does the stock market work as a mediating variable for shock transmission?
3. Is there any moderating impact of oil price on the dynamic conditional correlation (DCC) between the stock market and exchange rate?

For data analysis, I have checked other relevant literature.

For research question 1, most of them used the VAR model to check the direct influence of variables on each other. For research question 2, most of them used VAR Granger Causality and determined if the stock market transmits the shock as a mediating variable or not. I haven’t found any paper on my 3rd research question but a paper suggested a technique to address it in their future research question. I am giving their exact quotation, “The moderating effect of oil can be estimated by using the NARDL framework for studying the direct influence of OP on the DCCs between SI and ER”.

But the problem is that, for my 1st and 2nd, I can’t use the VAR model as I have autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity which I can’t remove even after log transforming or log differencing the variable. I also can’t use VECM Model either as my variables are not co-integrated from the Johansen co-integration test. Therefore give me a solution for my model. Which other econometric model can I use that takes autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity into account for my 1st and 2nd research questions as well as also give me guidelines on how to approach the analysis of my 3rd research question? I am really lost here. I don’t know how to analyze the process in R. And What about VAR-DCC-GARCH, I have seen some research paper used it. Does it suit my research question? If suited, include the R commands for VAR-DCC-GARCH too?

Tutor: Based on your data issues and research questions, I recommend using a GARCH model to take care of heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation problems, and VAR-DCC-GARCH may indeed suit your research questions. Let me provide you with an overview of how to approach this analysis.

1. For research question 1 and 2: To address heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation issues, you can use the GARCH (Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity) model. Since you want to study the "direct influence" and "Granger causality" among your variables, you can use a multivariate GARCH model. Specifically, you can apply the VAR-DCC-GARCH model that you mentioned, which enables you to estimate the time-varying correlations among your variables and determine the Granger causality as well. Additionally, residual cross-correlation analysis like Ljung-Box test can be employed to further verify the transmission effects after implementing VAR-DCC-GARCH model.

2. For research question 3: You can run a non-linear autoregressive distributed lag (NARDL) model to analyze the moderating effect of oil price on the dynamic conditional correlation between the stock market and exchange rate. This approach is advantageous since it allows you to capture possible asymmetric responses of the DCCs to positive and negative oil price changes. Therefore, using NARDL is suitable for your third research question.

Here's a general guideline on how to perform VAR-DCC-GARCH analysis in R using the "rmgarch" package (https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rmgarch):

1. Install and load the "rmgarch" package:

   ```R
   install.packages("rmgarch")
   library(rmgarch)
   ```

2. Prepare your data:

   ```R
   # Import your data, for example using read.csv()
   data <- read.csv("yourdata.csv")
   
   # Convert the data to a time series format using xts
   library(xts)
   data_xts <- xts(data[, 2:ncol(data)], order.by = as.Date(data[, 1]))
   
   # Take log returns (if needed)
   log_returns <- diff(log(data_xts))
   ```
   
3. Estimate the VAR-DCC-GARCH model:

   ```R
   # Specify a univariate GARCH(1,1) model for each series
   garchSpec <- ugarchspec(variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)))
   
   # Specify the DCC specification
   ```

6. Safety Management and accident prevention: The shipping industry is inherently risky, with the possibility of accidents causing significant loss of life, property, and environmental damage. Companies must continuously enhance safety management systems and procedures to minimize risks.

7. Cybersecurity: The growing reliance on digital systems and automation in the shipping industry increases vulnerability to cyberattacks. Companies must protect their networks, data, and critical infrastructure from cyber threats.

8. Geopolitical risks: Conflicts, political instability, and international sanctions can disrupt trade flows and create uncertainty for the shipping industry.

9. Changing trade patterns: Shifts in global trade patterns, such as the rise of China and other emerging markets, require the shipping industry to adapt and develop new routes and infrastructure networks.

10. Climate change: Severe weather and rising sea levels can affect shipping routes, port infrastructure, and the safety of maritime operations. The industry must find ways to adapt to these changes and minimize potential disruptions.

Tutor: Ladies and gentlemen,

Thank you for coming to this lecture on the fascinating topic of luminaries in the three Abrahamic faiths - Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

On the fourth day of creation described in the first chapter of Genesis, God created the luminaries in the firmament, which include the sun, the moon, and stars. These luminaries serve several purposes; they are meant "to separate the day from the night, and for signs, and times, and days, and years." I will now discuss the main interpretations of these signs as understood by the three Abrahamic faiths – Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

In Judaism, the signs mentioned in Genesis are primarily understood as the celestial bodies functioning to mark times for religious observances, such as the start and end of Sabbaths and festivals. For example, Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, is determined based on the appearance of the new moon. The luminaries' roles in guiding the cycles of time are, thus, a means of connecting God's creation with the practice of faith.

In Christianity, the signs take on a multi-layered symbolism. While the literal interpretation of dividing day from night and marking times for religious observance, such as Easter, is accepted, there is a deeper symbolism tied to the salvation story. In the Christian worldview, the luminaries represent God as the Light of the World. The sun is often associated with Christ, who brings light and salvation to humanity. The moon and stars are said to signify the Church, reflecting the light of Christ to the world. The movement of the celestial bodies also serves as a reminder of cycles of spiritual growth, including death and resurrection.

In Islam, the signs are understood similarly to Judaism and Christianity for marking times of prayer, fasting, and religious observance. Muslims also use the lunar calendar to determine the start of Ramadan - the holy month of fasting - as well as the timing of daily prayers. However, the Quran also highlights the importance of the luminaries as signs of God's existence, power, and presence in the natural world. In addition, the celestial bodies serve as reminders of God's guidance and protection for humanity, both in this life and the afterlife.

In summary, the luminaries created on the fourth day of creation play significant roles in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam as markers of time for religious observance, as well as symbols of God's divine order and guidance in the natural world. The three Abrahamic faiths share a deep appreciation and respect for the luminaries and the intricate, systematic design that they represent.

Student: Give a suitable, alluring and jargon and compact sub-heading in five six words                             While it may be tempting to believe that we are living in an era of globalization, characterised by rapid technological advancements, intensified cross-cultural exchanges, and the proliferation of knowledge systems, contemporary societies are still deeply rooted in Eurocentric frameworks of thinking. The long-lasting impact of colonialism, imperialism, and global power asymmetries continue to shape the cognitive, cultural, and social domains of academia, politics, and media. These influences propagate various orientalist stereotypes, oppressive binaries, and discriminatory practices that impede the development of a genuinely pluralistic and egalitarian world. Eurocentrism can be defined as an epistemological framework that situates European culture, history, and values as the defining center of the world, while at the same time disregarding or belittling the contributions of other cultures and civilisations. This ethnocentric positioning perceives the Europe or West as a paragon of universal values and cultural superiority, leading to a systematic undervaluation and misrepresentation of non-European cultures. Central to the Eurocentric paradigm is the construction of a dichotomy between the West and the so-called “non-West,” which is characterized by essentialist and often discriminatory distinctions between these two spheres. As noted by Edward Said (1979), this binary opposition manifests itself in various forms of discourse, such as history, literature, music and art, where non-European societies are stereotypically depicted as exotic, inferior, irrational, fanatic and backward in comparison to the civilised, rational, and progressive European model. European culture, according to him “gained strength and identity by setting itself off against the Orient as a sort of surrogate and even underground self.” (3) In other words, the Orient functions as a mirror to the West in that the West relies heavily on its counterpart, the Orient, for its own sense of superiority. (Sandy and Ouardi, 2019, p. 129) This paradigm, therefore, not only consolidates the stature of the West, but also perpetuates the subordination of non-European societies within global power structures, and the spheres of knowledge and influence. Said’s work on Orientalism provides a seminal critique of this discourse, demonstrating how its utilization has justified colonization, exploitation, and violence against Eastern civilizations.
	The Knowledge production or the representation of the Orient in Western narratives is not a recent development; it has existed since the earliest times. Edward Said traces the development of these knowledge-producing mechanisms, which Foucault referred to as “regimes of truths,” as far back as ancient Greece, with particular reference to two plays by Aeschylus. The early portrayals of the Orient as a “hostile other,” “a world beyond the seas” have evolved and expanded alongside colonial endeavours, with literary works often serving as propaganda tools to spread false images of the colonized territories. As Said writes, 
The “Orient was created -or, as I call it, “Orientalized”- and to believe that such things happen simply as a necessity of the imagination is to be disingenuous… The Orient was Orientalized not only because it was discovered to be “Oriental” in all those ways considered commonplace by an average nineteenth-century European, but also because it could be -that is, submitted to being- made Oriental.” (5-6)
Said also highlights the power imbalance between the West and the Orient as a critical factor in shaping these universalized images, which reinforce Western dominance. Essentially, the Orientalist discourse is contingent upon a distinct power dynamic that enables the West to create and maintain reductive images of the East. Exercising control over the Orient’s representation, the West situates itself as the observer, imbued with the power to discipline by defining what the East is and is not. The “power/knowledge” nexus – the notion that the production, dissemination, and control of knowledge serve as primary agents of power is reminiscent of the Panopticon, wherein the West becomes the observer, the bearer of the power-laden gaze, determining the Eastern identity, norms, morals and interests. This gaze reifies a grid of intelligibility that legitimates specific research as objective knowledge. Nevertheless, existing critiques of Orientalism seldom address the central role of gender in the construction of these discourses. As a consequence, the ways in which the gendered identities of colonised women have been manipulated to serve Western imperialist interests remain underexplored. As Ann Laura Stoler notes in her work Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2010), gender is often used as a tool for controlling and regulating colonised populations. Therefore, in response, this paper aims to extend Said’s analytical framework to incorporate the nexus between gender and imperialism, exploring how the Western discursive configuration of colonized women has reinforced and justified modes of subjugation and control.

Tutor: The paragraph presents a list of seven methods that are claimed to wear people out, lower their quality of life, and make them more self-conscious. While some of the mentioned factors can indeed affect one's mental well-being and overall quality of life, the paragraph seems to make sweeping generalizations and does not provide any concrete evidence to back up its claims. A thorough criticism of the core ideas would involve addressing the issues with each method:

1. Food and drinks: While it is true that consuming unhealthy food and drinks can negatively impact one's physical and mental health, the paragraph fails to differentiate between healthy and unhealthy choices, implying that all food and drinks hold negative effects.

2. Medication and health care: This point is highly problematic, as it seems to equate health care (including vitamins) with wearing people out and lowering their quality of life, which is contrary to the intended purpose of health care. Although overreliance on medication can be harmful, countless people benefit from accessing healthcare services and using medications as prescribed by professionals.

3. Electrical waves: It is true that excessive exposure to screens and electronic devices can negatively impact one's physical and mental health, but the paragraph fails to mention the benefits technology brings to our lives. It also seems to presume a conspiratorial intention behind the existence of electronic devices, without providing evidence for this view.

4. Media: While it is valid to say that the media can be biased, manipulative, or overstimulating, it is important to acknowledge that the media is a diverse landscape, with many valuable sources of information and entertainment as well. The paragraph does not make this distinction and instead implies that all media is harmful.

5. Music and sounds: It is unclear how the paragraph defines this method as distinct from media and why it considers music and sounds as inherently harmful. On the contrary, many studies have shown the positive effects music and sounds can have on individuals' emotional states and overall well-being.

6. Air pollution: Air pollution is a valid concern for public health, and it can indeed lower quality of life. However, the paragraph does not elaborate on how this relates to self-consciousness or how it is connected with the other methods listed.

7. Education system: The paragraph seems to dismiss almost all existing knowledge as "corrupt," which is an unwarranted generalization. Although it is important to question the knowledge we receive, completely dismissing all fields of study as harmful is simplistic and unproductive.

Overall, the paragraph promotes a pessimistic and conspiratorial view of the world, focusing on potentially negative aspects while neglecting the benefits and positive sides of various aspects of life. It lacks nuance and evidence, making it difficult to take its claims seriously.
